panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A is an axial CT of the head showing the right-sided complex fracture and malunion of the zygomaticomaxillary complex, matching the article's diagnosis. B: Panel B is a coronal CT view demonstrating the displacement and complex fracture pattern of the zygomaticomaxillary complex. C: Panel C is a sagittal CT view showing the malunited fracture of the zygomaticomaxillary complex and associated temporomandibular joint changes.

in_text_mentions: e right zygomatic arch and infraorbital rim. On intraoral examination, all sets of permanent teeth were present with bilaterally stable occlusion. Provisional diagnosis of malunited right zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture with ectropion with House-Brackmann grade IV facial nerve weakness was made. Radiological investigation included a CT scan of the head and face with three-dimensional reconstruction (Figures 2, 3). The CT revealed a malunited right zygomatic arch fracture along with a right zygomaticomaxillary buttress fracture, and an ankylotic mass over the right temporomandibular joint.

plate_findings.evidence: depressed zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture with loss of projection

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: CT scan of the maxillo-facial region demonstrating a visibly depressed zygomatic arch on the top-left quadrant. B: CT scan showing displacement at the sphenozygomatic suture visible in the top-right quadrant. C: CT scan showing minimal orbital floor displacement in the bottom-left quadrant, consistent with a complex zygomaticomaxillary fracture. D: CT scan visualization of the zygomaticomaxillary buttress in the bottom-right quadrant, showing signs of fracture/displacement as part of the complex fracture.

panels.figure_caption: Maxillofacial computed tomographic scan, demonstrating a depressed zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture with loss of projection (top left), displacement at the sphenozygomatic suture (top right), zygomaticomaxillary buttress (bottom right), with minimal orbital floor displacement (bottom left).
in_text_mentions: Reduction should be performed for displaced fractures that result in trismus, contour asymmetry, or significant orbital floor disruption (Fig 1).1 The zygomaticomaxillary buttress can be accessed through a gingivobuccal sulcus incision. This incision is typically made 5 mm superior to the mucogingival junction through mucosa and then periosteum. The risks of this incision are damage to the parotid papilla, which is typically located adjacent to the first or second maxillary molar, and damage to the infraorbital nerve.
